newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-News slumps on Heritage deal worries.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-News slumps on Heritage deal worries.

text.p: Shares in global media group News Corp Ltd slumped 22 cents or over three percent to A$6.36 in active early trade on Tuesday after it announced a US$1.35 billion deal to buy television and radio owner Heritage Media Corp.
News' shares fell in New York overnight as brokers and analysts questioned the effect on the News balance sheet of the continued buying spree.
News' preferred shares were hit hardest, falling 35 cents or over six percent to A$5.25 by 10.50 a.m. (2350 GMT) on further worries about dilution.

News said it would pay the equivalent of US$20.50 for each of Heritage's 38.6 million shares, or a total of US$754 million, by issuing the preferred limited voting ordinary shares. News Corp also will assume about $600 million in outstanding debt.
"The market hasn't taken it kindly," said Shaw Stockbroking dealer Jamie Spiteri. "It obviously has a short term effect because of the dilution of shares," he said.
U.S. investors pushed News' American Depositary Receipts (ADRs) down 3/8 to US$20.5 overnight, while the U.S. listed preference shares closed down 5/8 at 17 1/4.

Some brokers were however surprised at the extent of the selloff, given the widespread expectation that Rupert Murdoch's News would continue using the preference shares to expand News without diluting his own voting rights.
"Anybody who didn't expect these preference shares would be used again by Rupert to expand the capital base without diluting his voting rights is kidding themselves," said a Sydney broker.
"If anything the reaction is there because it wasn't expected," the broker said.

Heritage, based in Dallas, provides in-store marketing products and services for grocery, drug and mass merchandise outlets. It also operates six network-affiliated television stations and 24 radio stations in seven major markets.
News Corp said it planned to sell Heritage's radio and television broadcast properties and keep its marketing services operations, which would complement those of its own.

Heritage owns ACTMEDIA Inc, which provides in-store marketing products in more than 40,000 supermarkets, drug stores and mass merchandisers worldwide, and DIMAC Marketing Corp, a full-service, vertically integrated direct marketing services company.
News Corp, through News America FSI, publishes free-standing promotional inserts in the United States.
It produces more than 60 million weekly inserts, which are distributed in more than 600 Sunday newspapers throughout the country.

U.S. analysts said the acquisition of such Heritage units as ACTMEDIA, which provide products like coupons to drug stores and supermarkets, were a good fit for News Corp's free-standing inserts (FSI) business.
However, they questioned Murdoch's further investment in inserts and the effect News Corp's continuing buying spree would have on its balance sheet.
In the last year or so News Corp has spent about US$5 billion on purchases, including the US$2.8 billion acquisition of New World Communications Group Inc.
Most of the purchases have been paid for with stock.
